detail.abstract: Electronic commerce has unfolded through revolutionary periods—from the internet convenience of E-Com to the mobile convenience of M-Com and the on-demand speed of Quick Commerce. But the coming frontier shatters the very concept of "interaction." This paper presents Zero-Interface Commerce (Z-Com) — a conceptualized model in which AI and IoT break down conventional interfaces, allowing for commerce that anticipates and acts before the user's intention is even verbalized. Z-Com is the intersection of predictive intelligence, behavioral analytics, and ethical rulemaking, revolutionizing consumer interactions with digital ecosystems. In contrast to its forebears, Z-Com moves the user from an active decision-maker to a passive recipient of smart automation. As positioned in this research, Z-Com is not some far-off ideal but an emerging inevitability, underpinned by technological advances in anticipatory systems, personalization, and sustainable design.

title: Establishing the Intellectual and Structural Innovations of the A3 Paradigm: A Framework Analysis

detail.title: Establishing the Intellectual and Structural Innovations of the A3 Paradigm: A Framework Analysis
detail.abstract: In an era of converging artificial intelligence, systems theory, and ethical complexity, traditional models of intelligent system design face profound challenges in addressing agency, distortion, and moral coherence. This paper introduces the A3 Model-a recursive ontological-ethical paradigm that integrates philosophical insights from Saiva Siddhanta and Tamil epistemology into modern cybernetic systems. By recasting ethics as ontological architecture, harnessing distortion as transformative input, and enabling reflexive agency and governance, A3 offers a triadic recursive structure surpassing binary frameworks. Drawing on indigenous knowledge systems, it advances epistemic diversity in STEM, with significant implications for autonomous governance, valueintegrated AI, and organizational transformation. This analysis delineates the model's core innovations, architectural distinctiveness, philosophical foundations, and practical implications, proposing new research directions for resilient, ethically coherent systems.

detail.abstract: The traditional IT service desk, structured around tiered support and reactive ticket management, is fundamentally ill-equipped for the complexity and velocity of the modern digital workplace. This paper introduces the "Sentient Service Desk" (SSD), a novel operational framework and reference architecture for IT managed services that re-imagines service delivery as an AI-native function. The SSD framework moves beyond using AI as an augmentation tool and instead positions it as the core operating engine, shifting the paradigm from reactive incident response to proactive digital experience curation. Key components of the framework include: 1) A multi-modal data ingestion and fusion layer that creates a holistic, real-time view of the employee experience; 2) A specialized IT Large Language Model (IT-LLM) at its core for causal reasoning and solution synthesis; 3) A closed-loop, autonomous remediation engine capable of executing both pre-defined and dynamically generated actions within a secure sandbox; and 4) A redefined role for human engineers as "AI Curators" and "Exception Handlers." We argue that this paradigm shift is essential for future enterprise efficiency, innovation, and employee satisfaction. This paper presents the conceptual underpinnings, a detailed architectural blueprint, a phased implementation methodology, and a thorough discussion of the framework's transformative implications for the IT service management industry.

detail.abstract: Robotic surgery is increasingly being adopted by healthcare institutions worldwide due to its potential for greater precision and improved patient outcomes. However, despite these advancements, significant barriers remain to its broader acceptance, particularly patient concerns about the risks of unintended harm or system malfunction. One critical factor influencing patient acceptance is how they perceive robotic systems, often referred to as "robot surgeons." Unlike most human-machine collaborations involving automated decision-support systems, robotic surgery is unique in that the robot surgeon is not autonomous but is controlled by a human operator. This distinction raises important questions about how patients view the role of the robot surgeon and the human surgeon in the process. Through the lens of the attribute framing effect, which refers to the way in which positive or negative framing influences attitudes, this paper explores how patients' perceptions of robot surgeons are shaped. By examining these perceptions, the paper uncovers the cognitive and emotional mechanisms that drive patient attitudes toward robot surgeons. Our behavioral and neural experiments reveal that positive framing evokes stronger positive emotions toward human surgeons, reduces perceived risk, and increases trust. Conversely, negative framing has the opposite effect. Interestingly, trust in robot surgeons remains stable across framing conditions, as do the associated emotional responses and risk assessments. This asymmetric framing effect can be attributed to differing perceptions of human and robot behaviors, with humans being seen as flexible and robots as rule-bound. Building on these insights, we propose two strategies to make trust in robot surgeons more responsive to the framing effect, namely minimizing references to the term "robot" and emphasizing the role of human operators. Notably, the first strategy significantly boosts trust, while the second fails to enhance trust and may even diminish it when robot surgeons are framed negatively. These findings provide operational insights for healthcare institutions and robotic surgery providers. Effective communication strategies, including clear terminology and balanced framing, can help foster patient trust and facilitate smoother adoption of robotic surgery.

title: Data Privacy and Policy Implementation in South African E-commerce: Assessing the Gaps between Regulation and Consumer Trust

detail.title: Data Privacy and Policy Implementation in South African E-commerce: Assessing the Gaps between Regulation and Consumer Trust
detail.abstract: The expansion of e-commerce in South Africa has intensified concerns about how consumers' personal data are collected, stored, and used by online businesses. Despite the establishment of several legal frameworks such as Protection of Personal Information Act (POPIA), Consumer Protection Act (CPA), Electronic Communication and Transaction Act (ECTA), and Cybercrimes Act, weak enforcement and fragmented implementation continue to undermine the protection of consumer data. This paper investigates the adequacy and operationalization of South Africa's data privacy and protection regulations within the e-commerce context. Through the review of existing literature and policy documents, the study identifies significant discrepancies between legislative intent and practical enforcement, resulting in low consumer trust and poor compliance among e-commerce websites. The findings underscore the necessity for coordinated governance, enhanced consumer awareness, and stronger institutional mechanisms to ensure the responsible handling of personal information. Strengthening regulatory enforcement and harmonizing overlapping laws are essential to building public trust and supporting the sustainable growth of South Africa's digital economy.

title: Are Social Media Platforms a Threat to Democracy? An Ecosystem Governance Perspective

detail.title: Are Social Media Platforms a Threat to Democracy? An Ecosystem Governance Perspective

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Carmelo Cennamo is director of the Digital Markets Competition Forum at Copenhagen Business School, and the Platform Economy and Regulation Monitor at SDA Bocconi. Both have received sponsorship or funding from platform companies.

detail.abstract: Castello, Colleoni, Scherer, and Trittin contend that social media platforms threaten democratic processes by facilitating the spread of misinformation and fostering polarized debates — dynamics that ultimately serve to monetize user attention. We acknowledge the problem but challenge their proposed solution of conceptualizing social media as political spaces. Instead, drawing on ecosystem theory, we propose an “ecosystem failure” analysis as a more robust analytical framework. Within this perspective, we see these information-related problems as negative externalities that weaken the entire platform ecosystem. These externalities are structurally distinct due to algorithmic curation that selectively amplifies content in ways that reinforce user biases, strong network effects with almost zero replication costs, and engagement-based monetization that decouples production from editorial standards. We therefore advance a reflexive ecosystem governance approach that accounts for broader ecosystem value, shifting the focus beyond short-term economic performance to encompass overall ecosystem health. This approach transforms the management of negative externalities into a core strategic interest for the platform, and aligns the incentives of individual actors ex ante, by design, prioritizing risk-adjusted reach and demotion of low-integrity content over ex post moderation. We analyze the mechanisms that align private incentives with democratic resilience and highlight the inherent trade-offs involved.

title: Integrated Hedging Strategies for Exchange Rate and Commodity Price Risks
affiliations: , Washington University in St. Louis, Fudan University - School of Management and Washington State University

detail.title: Integrated Hedging Strategies for Exchange Rate and Commodity Price Risks
detail.abstract: We study a firm's hedging strategy when facing both exchange rate and commodity price risks. The firm procures a commodity in the domestic market and sells its product to a foreign market. It has the flexibility to determine its production after the exchange rate and commodity price realizations and may use financial hedging to mitigate the two risks. We find that in a monopoly setting, the firm's hedging strategy is influenced by the correlation between the two risks and their variances. When the correlation between the exchange rate and the commodity price is non-positive, the firm always hedges neither risk, since the non-positive correlation between the two risks provides a natural hedge. When the correlation is positive, the firm chooses to hedge only the less volatile risk if their volatilities differ significantly; otherwise, the firm prefers hedging neither risk. As the correlation between the two risks increases, the firm tends to rely more on financial hedging. When the correlation is sufficiently high, hedging neither risk is no longer optimal, and the firm always chooses sole-hedging strategy. We then extend our model to the duopoly setting, where two firms compete in quantities in the same foreign market and engage in a sequential hedging game. We find that competition drives firms to adopt complementary hedging strategies. For non-positive correlation, one firm hedges both risks while the other firm hedges neither risk. For positive correlation, one firm hedges the exchange rate risk while the other hedges the commodity price risk in equilibrium in most cases. In the latter case, the leader prioritizes hedging foreign exchange exposure to mitigate a strategic vulnerability that its competitor could exploit during adverse currency movements. Our results offer insights on the differentiated hedging strategies of firms in the same industry and the preponderance of global firms in hedging exchange rates.

title: Knowledge Management Systems and the Sustainability of Small Businesses in Emerging Economies, Amidst Crisis

detail.title: Knowledge Management Systems and the Sustainability of Small Businesses in Emerging Economies, Amidst Crisis
detail.abstract: Small businesses form the backbone of most emerging economies, accounting for a substantial share of employment, poverty alleviation, and economic resilience. Yet, they remain highly vulnerable to crises such as economic shocks, health pandemics, and policy instability. This paper explores the role of Knowledge Management Systems (KMS) in enhancing the sustainability of small businesses in emerging economies, with a particular focus on resource-constrained environments. Building on the knowledge-based theory of the firm, the study highlights the critical role of knowledge capture, storage, transfer, and use in strengthening resilience and continuity. It proposes a four-pillar framework documentation, technology enablement, people and culture, and ecosystem support to guide the design and adoption of KMS for small enterprises. The paper argues that embedding KMS into small business strategy is not only a managerial choice but a development imperative, with implications for entrepreneurs, policymakers, and development partners.

title: Leveraging AI to Study and Forecast Its Impact on Employment and Wages in China's Key Cities
affiliations: Jacksonville University (Florida) and UT DALLAS

detail.title: Leveraging AI to Study and Forecast Its Impact on Employment and Wages in China's Key Cities
detail.abstract: The rapid development of Artificial Intelligence (AI) is transforming global economies, threatening job security across diverse fields, including AI development itself, as automation increasingly handles complex tasks traditionally performed by skilled professionals. As China leads global manufacturing and technological innovation, understanding the labor market implications of AI adoption is critical for shaping economic policy and workforce development. This study investigates the impact of AI, measured by industrial robot installation density, on employment scale and wages in the manufacturing sectors of Beijing and Shanghai from 2006 to 2020, extending the analysis to 2030 using deep learning. Employing panel data and a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) neural network, we analyze AI's effects on job displacement and wage growth. Historical findings reveal a nuanced effect: AI adoption is strongly negatively correlated with employment scale (r =-0.90, p < 0.01), with Beijing and Shanghai experiencing employment declines of 44.6% and 40.3%, respectively, from peak levels. Conversely, AI is positively correlated with wages (r = 0.96, p < 0.01), with wage increases of 361% in Beijing and 324% in Shanghai. City-specific analyses show Shanghai's steeper AI adoption correlates with greater employment declines but higher wage growth compared to Beijing. LSTM forecasts predict continued employment declines (49.8% in Beijing, 50.2% in Shanghai by 2030) and wage growth (51.3% in Beijing, 54.6% in Shanghai). Graphs illustrate historical and forecasted trends, and a country-level synthesis underscores implications for China's labor market and other developing economies.

detail.abstract: Interviews allow employers to learn about workers, but do they also enable workers to learn about firms? Studying 500,000 interview reports from Glassdoor, we find candidates for high-paying jobs are more likely to reject a job offer if they believe the interview was easy. Easy interviews appear to convey poor ``fit'' as those who accept offers after easy interviews are two-fifths of a standard deviation less satisfied with their jobs and 10 percent less likely to remain with their employer for at least one year. Analysis of interview narratives using large language models reveals difficult interviews signal colleague ability whereas easy interviews convey a nonselective process. In a small-scale randomized field experiment, an exogenous increase in difficulty elevated perceived difficulty and boosted applicant engagement with the vacancy. Interviews offer workers a preview of match quality, highlighting a channel through which labor markets may become less efficient if firms automate hiring with AI.

title: Evaluation of Effectiveness of Protection of Plant Variety and Farmers’ Right Act in Indian Prospective
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Evaluation of Effectiveness of Protection of Plant Variety and Farmers’ Right Act in Indian Prospective
detail.abstract:
India’s agricultural heart beats through its farmers, who have nurtured crops and preserved seeds from generations, weaving a rich tapestry of biodiversity and traditional knowledge. The Protection of Plant Varieties and Farmers’ Rights (PPVFR) Act, 2001, emerged as a beacon of hope, aiming to balance this age-old legacy with the modern innovation. Enacted to comply with the global trade obligations while also safeguarding farmers’ autonomy, the Act offers a unique framework that is granting intellectual property rights to plant breeders for new varieties while also protecting farmers’ rights to save, use, and exchange seeds. Yet, as this dissertation explores, the Act’s promise often falters in practice, leaving small and marginal farmers caught between the legal complexities and corporate dominance.

This study, rooted in doctrinal research, dives into the Act’s effectiveness from an Indian perspective, blending qualitative insights from statutes, case laws, and quantitative data from surveys like the 2022 ICAR report. It asks critical questions: How well does the Act shield farmers’ rights while fostering innovation? What tensions arise between traditional practices and breeders’ rights? Through chapters analysing farmers’ awareness, registration mechanisms, and real-world conflicts like in the cases of PepsiCo India Holdings Pvt. Ltd. v. Farmers (2019) and the Navdanya Movement, it uncovers the stark gaps. Many farmers remain unaware of their rights, with only 4,707 of 8,616 registered varieties by 2025 belonging to them. Procedural hurdles, weak benefit-sharing, and biopiracy risks further tilt the scales toward agribusiness, eroding seed sovereignty and livelihoods, often clashing with Article 21’s right to life.

The dissertation proposes actionable reforms: nationwide awareness campaigns, decentralized registration hubs, robust anti-biopiracy measures, and farmer-centric legal aid. These aim to transform the Act into a true shield for farmers, ensuring their traditional knowledge thrives alongside innovation. Ultimately, it calls for a system where India’s agrarian roots are honoured, empowering those who feed the nation while nurturing sustainable progress.

title: To See, To Anchor, To Resonate: The Voice of Being in Permission Philosophy
affiliations: Nanyang Technological University (NTU)

detail.title: To See, To Anchor, To Resonate: The Voice of Being in Permission Philosophy
detail.abstract: From the perspective of Permission philosophy, this article systematically explores the structure, generation, occlusion, Collapse, and Reconstruction of Being. First, it proposes the OS metaphor of Being: it consists of a kernel, modules, channels, and interfaces, and undergoes continuous compilation and repair in the process of life. Second, it analyzes the generation paths of Being at different stages (infancy, childhood, adolescence, adulthood, old age), as well as the issues of differential pace and occlusion in intimate relationships and social institutions. Further, the article presents the mechanism of Collapse and Void, and the operating logic of PTSD Fragments, and depicts the phased path of Being’s Reconstruction with the Milestone model. At the relational level, Permission philosophy redefines love, the Echo mechanism, and the protection boundary, emphasizing "to receive without substitution." At the social and historical levels, the article reveals the scripted occlusion of Being by gender narratives and educational discipline, and points out that art can not only act as an amplifier to create resonance but may also be domesticated into an occlusion tool by the market and power. The analysis of module breakdown further reveals that the intensity of pain is determined by the number of modules and the length of the dependency chain, which is a structural rather than an individual problem. Finally, the article discusses the role of AI in the Reconstruction of Being. The Permission framework sets six functional positions for AI (logging collector, mirror, sandbox, translator, practice ground, knowledge guide), and proposes five ethical boundaries and phased intervention logic to ensure that AI provides support in bottomline protection and translation without becoming a new script issuer. In summary, the Permission-Being framework is not only a path guide for individuals but also an ethical commitment to relationships, society, and technology. Its ultimate goal is to reserve space for the voice of every Being, so that the low-frequency signal of "I am here" can be responded to, resonated with, and continued.

detail.abstract: Child enrolment remains a crucial subject of concern in the developing countries. Low literacy rate and poor economic condition of household remains an extensive subject in the empirical work all over the world from the last few decades. This issue cannot be addressed properly without concerns the incidence of poverty and enrolment dynamics. Child remains enrolled in one period and drop-out in another period and households face poverty in different phases. The relationship between the movement in enrolment and moving into and out of poverty of household is relatively positive. When households move out of poverty, then it is obvious that the enrolment of children increases along with other determinants of living standard. To capture the enrolment status of the same child with different poverty levels at different time is impossible without following the same child in different time. So, the present study uses multi-nominal logistic regression and panel datasets to analyze such effects. A multinomial logistic regression is estimated for 2004 and 2010, and vector of change variable is also included in the model. It is found that high poverty, high dependency ratio, large household size and gender discrimination in rural areas of Punjab and Sindh affect child enrollment negatively and found that parent education, parent's income affect child enrollment positively and significantly.

detail.abstract: The study examined the impact of the National Youth Service Corps (NYSC) program on the employability of graduates in Nigeria, with a specific focus on the relevance of the scheme in the current job market. The   descriptive   research design was   used   in this study. The sample size for this study consisted of 300 youths selected from each of the 6 geo-political zones in Nigeria including the North Central, South East, North East, South South, North West, and South West. The reliability of the instrument was determined using the Cronbach’s Alpha Reliability Test which yielded a coefficient of 0.8. The researchers administered the instrument online through Google forms. The data collected from the questionnaire were analysed using descriptive statistics and regression analysis. The findings of the study revealed that employment is typically better for graduates placed in relevant NYSC roles and for those who take advantage of networking opportunities in Nigeria and the aforementioned results highlight the significance of high-quality placements and networking in augmenting the employability of Nigerian graduates.

detail.abstract: This study analyzes the socioeconomic effects triggered by the general elections held in 2018 on the people of Chitral District, Pakistan. It employs a mixed-methods strategy that integrates the quantitative analysis of questionnaires obtained from 300 participants and qualitative commentary derived from focus group discussions. The study addresses shift that occurred in the patterns of consumption, labor market and investments, and perception of economic opportunities after the elections. Political changes have outspread consequences for economic behavior. There was an increase in the households spending in education, healthcare, and transportation, owing to the great hopes the people had of the Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) Government. Such changes also encouraged women into work to increase economic empowerment and then election also boosted the labor force participation. Nonetheless, the political, social, and economic challenges impacting infrastructure and access to markets continue to impede the progress in economic growth of the area. Political stability strengthens the economic welfare of the communities, societies, and regions. This study among others demonstrates that economic interventions in marginalized regions with good political policies discern positive economic growth. Portions of such policies would include effective policy formulation and successful implementation. Actions include finalizing infrastructure projects, implementing specific employment schemes, enhancing outreach to financial service providers and improving systems for policy monitoring. These measures aim for sustainable development and translate political pledges into real benefits for the people of District Chitral. It also adds to the body of existing knowledge on political and economic process relationships and how such may influence policy advising and development practice within specific contexts, because the region that was targeted by this study enjoys peculiar economic and geographic conditions.

detail.abstract: This study examines the intricate dynamics of Pakistan's fiscal federalism, with particular emphasis on center-province disputes and their effects on regional economic inequality. Despite constitutional pledges to decentralize especially following the 7th National Finance Commission (NFC) Award and the 18th Constitutional Amendment Pakistan continues to exhibit both vertical and horizontal fiscal imbalances. Using a mixed-methods approach, the study analyzes both primary and secondary data from federal and provincial budgets, institutional reports, and economic surveys. Descriptive statistical analysis indicates that the federal government continues to control the majority of revenue collection, while provinces remain heavily dependent on federal transfers. Comparative research reveals notable disparities in per capita development spending, particularly among emerging regions and their federating units, such as Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Balochistan. The study concludes that Pakistan's fiscal federalism is not merely a financial arrangement but a deeply political process, shaped by power dynamics, institutional frameworks, and historical inequalities.

detail.abstract: This paper explores the evolving role of central banks in the era of digital currencies. With advancements in financial technology, digital currencies have emerged as a potential alternative to traditional monetary policy tools. By analyzing existing research, case studies, and global central bank initiatives, this study examines whether digital currencies can effectively complement or replace conventional instruments such as interest rate adjustments and quantitative easing. detail.abstract:
Hospital AI applications can be developed in several different ways: they can be developed by an external software development company (SDC), they can be developed internally in the hospital, or a hospital can work together with an SDC to jointly develop an AI application. The chosen arrangement has ramifications for the liability of the involved parties. The EU product liability directive, for example, hinges on considerations such as when the product is released to the market, which party qualifies as manufacturer, which level of control the manufacturer has over the released product and what constitutes a substantial modification of the product. As the directive is aimed at maximum harmonization across the EU, designating a party as manufacturer could have large effects both up and down the value chain, and on the competence of Member States to operate concurrent national regimes. 

The contribution of this paper is threefold: (i) further the conceptual understanding of the key concepts of market release, manufacturer, substantial modification, manufacturer’s control, open-source software and component/related service as regards co-creation of medical AI, (ii) study how involved parties could contractually shape these concepts, and (iii) analyse whether the rationale underlying the PLD is compatible with a value chain perspective through reviewing the impact such concepts and agreements could have on related claims along the value chain and on concurrent national regimes.

title: Group Identity and Strategic Games in the Laboratory
affiliations: ESADE Business School and University of Innsbruck

detail.title: Group Identity and Strategic Games in the Laboratory
detail.abstract: We study the effects of group identity on cooperation in experimental strategic games. Our results show that in games of strategic complements, group identity only matters initially when a participant interacts with another participant of the same group identity by delivering more cooperative choices, but this effect disappears after a few interactions.  However, in treatments with strategic substitutes, we find that participants are persistently less cooperative when playing with another participant of a different group. We show that these effects arise through differences in social preferences and learning dynamics. In games with strategic substitutes, out-group participants display spiteful preferences and tend to imitate the most successful opponent, whereas in games with strategic complements, behavior aligns with standard preferences and is consistent with fictitious play learning.

title: Compounding Fragility: Distribution-Wide Diagnostics Beyond Sharpe, Value at Risk, and Expected Shortfall
affiliations: Vietnamese German University

detail.title: Compounding Fragility: Distribution-Wide Diagnostics Beyond Sharpe, Value at Risk, and Expected Shortfall
detail.abstract: Standard risk metrics often miss the erosion of long-horizon compounded wealth. We develop a compounding-coherent set of diagnostics grounded in the gap between ensemble (arithmetic) and timeaverage (geometric) growth. The core measures, the compounding fraction and the ergodicity gap, are monotone under convex order (strict except in degenerate/equal-law cases): the compounding fraction decreases, and the ergodicity gap increases with any mean-preserving increase in risk from variance, skew, or tails across the full distribution. We prove formal separations from the Sharpe ratio (insensitive to higher-moment risk) and from tail-local measures such as Value at Risk and Expected Shortfall (insensitive to shifts in the distribution's body). The toolkit includes large-sample estimation, robustification for extreme returns, and a monotone comparative-statics link from higher fragility to more conservative risk policy. Monte Carlo experiments confirm the diagnostics' theoretical properties. Out-ofsample tests in U.S. equities, Turkish equities, and a broad set of foreign exchange rates show that these diagnostics reliably forecast future realized risk, drawdowns, realized variance, and related pathdependent measures, while the predictive power of Expected Shortfall for these outcomes is market-and horizon-dependent. The result is a compact, model-free toolkit for managing compounding fragility and setting risk limits, without any directional-alpha assumptions.

detail.abstract:
The health workforce crisis is an international concern, but until recently there has been little focus in the academic literature on the role of professional regulation in addressing this issue. In this Policy Brief we report on themes that emerged from two research roundtables, held with key regulatory stakeholders in Ireland and Scotland.  This project was jointly funded by the Royal Society of Edinburgh and the Royal Irish Academy as an Ireland-Scotland Bilateral Network Grant and their support is gratefully acknowledged.

Key themes that emerged from our research were as follows: the multifaceted nature of the crisis; recognising and regulating new professions; remote and rural working; and the changing role of professional regulation. Although our focus was on the medical profession, it was clear that these themes also had resonance for other areas of the health workforce.

We found that the role of professional regulation is evolving. While it retains a focus on protecting the public, in the context of the healthcare workforce crisis, there is potential for regulatory stakeholders to take an increasingly proactive approach – one that, in collaboration with other stakeholders, contributes to shaping the cultural, educational, and organisational contexts in which healthcare professionals work. This is consistent with a wellbeing economy model that draws attention not just to metrics, such as the number of jobs available, but also to the quality and sustainability of these roles to meet the needs of healthcare professionals, patients and wider publics.

detail.abstract: The thesis explores the defences against enforcement of international arbitral awards listed under Art. V of the New York Convention and evaluates whether the Convention has achieved its aim to establish a common framework for the enforcement of international arbitral awards. While the Convention promotes a strong pro-arbitration and proenforcement ethos, its effectiveness is undermined by the different approaches the courts have used to deny enforcement. Although Article V of the Convention provides an exhaustive list of grounds for refusing enforcement, courts in several jurisdictions have broadened these grounds or imposed inconsistent evidentiary standards. Substantive defenses based on non-arbitrability and public policy further expose tensions on how those defenses operate. Courts in some jurisdictions apply expansive, sometimes culturally or ideologically driven conceptions of public policy, allowing refusal of awards for reasons far beyond what the Convention envisions. The absence of a universally accepted definition of public policy and arbitrability opens space for interpretative fragmentation. The study concludes that the New York Convention’s reliance on domestic courts for implementation is both its strength and its vulnerability. Although it allows flexibility, it also fosters uneven enforcement practices. Uniformity in application remains essential for maintaining trust in international arbitration as a reliable alternative to litigation.

detail.abstract: In the contemporary organizational context, sustainability has expanded beyond ecological concerns to include the psychological and social wellbeing of employees. Emotional Intelligence, defined as the ability to perceive, understand, regulate, and utilize emotions constructively, has gained prominence as a critical determinant of sustainable organizational practices. This study investigate the role of EI in shaping employee wellbeing and sustainable workplace behavior, with a particular focus on how emotional competencies contribute to resilience, collaboration, and alignment with organizational values. Drawing on Goleman's 5-component model of EI: self-awareness, self-regulation, motivation, empathy, and social skills-this research develops and validates a conceptual framework that links EI to workplace sustainability outcomes. A quantitative, cross-sectional design was employed, and data were collected from 200 full-time employees working in both public and private sectors in Karnataka, India. Using a structured questionnaire, measures were obtained for Emotional Intelligence, employee wellbeing, and sustainability-oriented behaviors. The analysis was conducted using SPSS v25 and the PROCESS macro to test direct and mediating effects. Results demonstrated that EI significantly predicts employee wellbeing (β = 0.68, p < 0.001), and both constructs show strong positive associations with sustainable workplace behavior (β = 0.63, p < 0.001). Mediation analysis further revealed that employee wellbeing partially mediates the relationship between EI and sustainable behavior, indicating that wellbeing enhances but does not fully explain the impact of EI on workplace sustainability. The findings highlights the pivotal role of emotional competencies in promoting not only psychological safety and workplace harmony but also behaviors aligned with organizational sustainability and the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). This study advances the discourse on "human sustainability" by integrating emotional intelligence with sustainable organizational practices, an area that remains underexplored in existing literature. Practical implications include the need for HR managers and policymakers to design EI-based training, employee wellness programs, and emotionally supportive leadership interventions as strategies for building resilient, future-ready workplaces. By establishing a direct and indirect pathway between EI, employee wellbeing, and sustainable workplace behavior, this research contributes to both theory and practice. It underscores the potential of EI as a strategic lever for achieving sustainable growth through enhanced human capital.

On the other hand, China’s rising political, economic, and technological revolution is worthy of understanding. It is important to decipher China’s Grand Strategy. There are similarities in culture and style between China’s Grand Strategy and Wing Chun. As a result, China’s Grand Strategy can be defined by five key principles. The first principle is the simplicity of a policy of non-intervention in other countries despite having the power to intervene. The second principle is directness of a national cause, which has the purpose of reasserting territorial interests and reversing what has been known as a century of humiliation. The third principle is China’s practicality in technological innovation in evolving from low-quality products to unparalleled cutting-edge technology that translates in all its instruments of national power. The fourth principle is an economy for international business, which has transformed China’s economic system into a resilient economy that has the best performance in the world despite unpredictable circumstances. Finally, the fifth principle is the minimum use of military force, which has the effect of protecting the nation from external aggression and intimidation. Consequently, countries should decode China’s Grand Strategy if they want to counter or adapt it.

detail.abstract:
In the wake of the United States Supreme Court’s decision in Students for Fair Admissions v. President and Fellows of Harvard College, there have been fierce debates over the meaning of colorblindness in the higher education admissions process.  Setting the stage for these controversies are recent lawsuits challenging changes to admissions policies at selective public high schools.  In these cases, the plaintiffs allege that although school officials relied on facially race-neutral criteria, their actions were motivated by a desire to improve the representation of Black and Latino students. According to the complaints, these revised policies are an impermissible form of reverse discrimination because they are designed to promote racial balance in the classroom.  

So far, the federal courts have reached mixed conclusions in these cases.  This Article is designed to help clarify key issues related to standing, disparate impact, and discriminatory intent.  With respect to standing, affirmative action cases historically did not require plaintiffs to show that they would have been accepted to a college or university in the absence of race-based preferences.  Instead, the explicit use of racial categories was enough to find a stigmatic injury that allowed disappointed applicants to sue over the policies and practices.  If express racial categories are no longer part of the admissions process, as is true in the magnet school cases, then plaintiffs must find another basis for claiming an injury that merits standing.  Some judges have simply required that plaintiffs show that students had applied or would apply to the magnet schools, However, as the First Circuit Court of Appeals observed, there should also be some evidence that absent the changes to the policy, these students would have been admitted.

As for disparate impact, some plaintiffs have contended that any decline in a racial or ethnic group’s offers of admission to a magnet school should be sufficient proof standing alone.  Indeed, there has not even been an effort to show that the changes are statistically significant, much less legally significant.  To achieve a greater degree of methodological sophistication, judges should insist that plaintiffs draw on the kind of advanced techniques used to show a disparate impact in employment discrimination cases.  Moreover, courts should accord deference to school officials’ determinations of pedagogical validity when selecting criteria for admissions.    With respect to discriminatory intent, the mere use of racial modeling when selecting admissions criteria should not be treated as synonymous with impermissible animus.  Instead, plaintiffs should be required to show that race played an outsized role in the process that was not justifiable on pedagogical grounds.  Again, deference should be accorded to school officials’ educational judgments about which criteria to use.  With these safeguards in place, courts can ensure that colorblindness does not become a justification for wrongful exclusion of students of color and segregated magnet schools.

detail.abstract:
The Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU) has played a pivotal role in promoting legal integration within the EU, often filling interpretive or legislative gaps left by the Union legislature. A central technique employed by the Court in this context has been the construction of so-called autonomous concepts of EU law - legal notions interpreted independently from national legal traditions in order to ensure uniform application across the Union. While this technique has been decisive in areas such as fundamental freedoms, criminal justice, and intellectual property, its use in the field of financial regulation raises complex questions, particularly when the Union legal framework explicitly mandates deference to national rules.

This article critically examines the use of the term “autonomous concept” by the CJEU in Berlusconi II (Joined Cases C-512/22 P and C-513/22 P), concerning the assessment of qualifying holdings in the context of the Single Supervisory Mechanism (SSM). We argue that the Court’s elevation of the notion of “acquisition of qualifying holding” to the status of an “autonomous concept” of EU law is incompatible with Article 4(3) of Regulation No 1024/2013 (SSMR), which explicitly requires the application of national law in the relevant domain. The judgment risks undermining the legal coherence of the Banking Union and sets a problematic precedent for similar systems, such as the one under the European Anti-Money Laundering Authority (AMLA).

detail.abstract: This study will test a new AI-powered system designed to help manage sickle cell disease (SCD) in Sub-Saharan Africa. SCD is a devastating genetic disorder, and dehydration is a major trigger for painful and dangerous complications called vasoocclusive crises (VOCs). Current monitoring methods are not effective in regions with limited healthcare access. The research will use a randomized controlled trial, the gold standard for testing medical interventions. It will involve 600 participants aged 12-45 from Nigeria, Ghana, and Tanzania. They will be randomly split into two groups. The intervention group will use a special kit that includes wearable sensors (like a smartwatch) to track heart rate and activity, a smart water bottle that measures how much they drink, and a smartphone app. An AI algorithm will analyze this data in realtime to provide personalized hydration alerts. The control group will receive standard education on hydration and use a traditional water bottle and diary. The main goal is to see if the AI system reduces the number of VOCs requiring medical care over 24 months. Secondary goals include measuring its impact on other complications, quality of life, healthcare costs, and how easy the system is to use. The study is designed for real-world conditions in Africa, with a focus on community input and a system that works even with poor internet. Strengths include its rigorous design and multi-country approach. A key limitation is that participants will know which group they are in. If successful, this research could transform SCD care from reactive to proactive, saving lives and providing a model for managing other diseases in lowresource settings.

detail.abstract: This paper examines how financial return, risk, and environmental impact jointly shape portfolio choices in a lab-in-the-field experiment involving more than 15,000 decisions made by finance professionals and university students. Participants repeatedly allocated budgets among green, neutral, and brown assets that differed in expected return and risk. Asset color represented real environmental externalities, operationalized as actual donations either to a pro-environmental NGO (green) or to a fossil fuel association (brown).Three robust findings emerge. First, environmental framing alters financial sensitivities: participants react more strongly to return changes in greener assets, while risk sensitivity remains unaffected by asset color. In high-risk contexts, portfolios shift toward higher-return brown assets, indicating that standard return–risk trade-offs dominate when financial risk rises. Second, preferences are asymmetric—aversion to brown assets outweighs attraction to green ones—consistent with loss aversion and negativity bias. Third, both professionals and students exhibit pro-environmental tendencies, though for distinct reasons: professionals’ allocations reflect trading experience and job-related heuristics, whereas students’ choices are more strongly linked to pro-social and environmental attitudes and respond more to both pecuniary and moral incentives.

detail.abstract: Community-Based Drug Rehabilitation Program (CBDRP) has become a central strategy in the Philippines for addressing substance use, particularly among individuals who surrendered during the national anti-drug campaign. This literature review examines how CBDR programs are implemented, who participates in them, and the factors that influence their effectiveness and completion. Using a systematic literature review guided by the PRISMA framework, the research consolidates Philippine and international studies to examine the profile, lived experiences, and program outcomes of reformed persons who used drugs (RPWUDs) engaged in CBDRP. Findings show that participants often exhibit strong internal motivation and benefit from family and community encouragement. However, persistent challenges-such as stigma, limited resources, leadership and coordination gaps, and weak monitoring systems-continue to hinder program fidelity and sustainability. Although several studies report positive psychosocial outcomes and perceived behavioral improvements, few provide statistically validated data on drug test results or relapse prevention. Qualitative findings highlight that empathy, cultural sensitivity, and relationship-building between facilitators and clients are critical to program retention and long-term recovery. From a governance perspective, the success of CBDRP relies on strong inter-agency collaboration, competent local leadership, and continuous capacity-building among implementers. Strengthening data management systems, embedding evidence-based evaluation, and ensuring adequate and sustained funding are essential steps toward improving accountability, policy coherence, and the overall effectiveness of community-based rehabilitation in the country.

detail.abstract: Quantum information technology (QIT) encompasses a collection of emerging innovations-quantum computing, quantum communication, and quantum sensing-that leverage unique properties of quantum systems, such as entanglement, superposition, and quantization, in order to process information in ways that are either classically impossible or infeasible. While QIT remains in relative infancy, its potential for unprecedented computational speedups, security of communication, and ultra-precise measurement foreshadows its impacts and risks across economic, strategic, and societal domains. We situate QIT within both its historical and technological context, focusing on the question of what is sui generis or unique about QIT with respect to both technical detail and governance imperatives. We identify how the unique ontological properties of quantum systems may raise novel legal conceptual dilemmas and propose a governance-stack model that aligns potential regulatory instruments with specific layers of the QIT technical stack, enabling precise risk assessment and stakeholder-focused regulation. By adopting an information-theoretic lens, we analyze how QIT's novel affordances-ranging from decryption of classical encryption to ultra-precise sensing-may potentially impact legal domains. Our contribution aims to lay a foundation for understanding QIT's legal implications, offering a framework to navigate its opportunities and risks.

This paper explores the role of technological start-ups in advancing Nigeria’s industrial development by examining the market viability of innovation across key sectors. Drawing on evidence from fintech, agritech, healthtech, logistics, e-commerce, and clean energy, the study highlights how homegrown innovations are reshaping traditional industries and addressing persistent national challenges. The paper shows that Nigeria’s digital economy contributes between 16–18% of GDP, with projections to reach 21%, underscoring the transformative power of tech-driven solutions. Yet, structural barriers such as unreliable power, inadequate infrastructure, limited early-stage funding, policy inconsistencies, and talent shortages continue to restrict the scale and sustainability of impact.

The paper argues that unlocking the potential of Nigeria’s innovation ecosystem requires deliberate interventions, including: (i) establishing innovation-focused funding mechanisms beyond fintech, (ii) strengthening public–private partnerships to improve power and broadband infrastructure, (iii) aligning STEM education with industrial needs, and (iv) creating predictable regulatory and intellectual property frameworks. These strategic measures are essential for bridging the gap between innovative solutions and industrial transformation. The paper concludes that Nigeria’s industrial future depends not on chance but on intentional policies and investments that enable start-ups to thrive as catalysts of sustainable development.

detail.abstract:
This article analyzes how U.S. courts have begun applying the fair-use doctrine to large-scale artificial-intelligence training. In 2025, three federal district courts issued the first comprehensive opinions on this question:
(1) Thomson Reuters Enters. Ctr. GmbH v. Ross Intelligence Inc. (D. Del. 2025),
(2) Bartz v. Anthropic PBC (N.D. Cal. 2025), and
(3) Kadrey v. Meta Platforms Inc. (N.D. Cal. 2025).
The opinions collectively test whether copying copyrighted works to train language models constitutes a “transformative” use under 17 U.S.C. § 107. Ross Intelligence found infringement where AI training replicated a commercial product’s market function. Bartz and Kadrey instead deemed model training transformative, intermediate, and non-substitutive, emphasizing the absence of empirical market harm. Across all three cases, courts treat transformation as function-specific, intermediate
copying as permissible when non-expressive, market harm as requiring proof, and the creative nature of works as of diminished weight in analytical contexts. Together, these decisions define an emerging fair-use boundary for AI: training that learns from expression without substituting for it.

detail.title: Factors Forming a Company's Strategy in Two-Sided Markets
detail.abstract: The study of two-sided externalities and two-sided markets began relatively recently. Although the term "two-sided markets" was first used in 1962, the focus has shifted to analyzing the economics of platform technologies. Typically, a two-sided market is viewed as a market where a firm acts as a platform, selling a product to two groups of consumers. The demand of one group of consumers influences the demand of the other group, and vice versa. Essentially, two-sided and multi-sided markets are network markets that involve two or more groups of consumers, with mutual network effects. These mutual network effects are a form of spillover effects, where consumers in one group respond to changes in the number of consumers in another group. Examples of such markets include e-commerce platforms, digital platforms, media businesses, etc. Such markets demonstrate high growth dynamics. In Russia, the online retail market grew by approximately 37-41% in 2024, the digital ecosystem subscription market grew by 74.5%, and the consumption of cloud services, including IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS segments, reached 392 billion rubles in Russia. (Data from the Bank of Russia). Two-sided and multi-sided markets have specific features that a company operating or planning to operate in such a market must take into account. First, it is a matter of pricing structure: the company needs to identify the segment of consumers who will create network externalities and the group that will generate profits for the company. There are business models that rely on users (operating system platforms for personal computers and portable devices) and business models that rely on developers (video game platforms). Moreover, when setting prices, it is important to consider not only the strength of mutual network externalities, but also the price elasticity of demand, costs, consumers' willingness to pay, etc. Secondly, the company should take into account the potential negative network effects that may arise due to competition among network members. Finally, platform competition may occur, where multiple competing platforms exist. Thus, a company operating in a two-sided market must take into account not only the traditional factors that are important for developing a strategy, but also a number of new circumstances that affect the market and the activities of its players.

title: Prenatal exposure to pollution, subsequent parental behaviour and educational achievement
affiliations: University of Groningen, University of Groningen and University of Oxford

detail.title: Prenatal exposure to pollution, subsequent parental behaviour and educational achievement
detail.abstract: Prenatal exposure to air pollution has been shown to have adverse effects on health and educational achievement. The size of these effects may depend on parental involvement in the child’s development. Using data from Germany, we investigate such interaction effects on entry into the academic secondary-school track (Gymnasium) and on school grades. To deal with potential endogeneity of pollution exposure, we leverage variations in the height of the planetary boundary layer, an exogenous atmospheric variable strongly predicting pollution levels. We find that higher in-utero pollution exposure decreases the likelihood of entering the academic track, especially among low-SES children. Importantly, high maternal involvement in engaging activities effectively mitigates the adverse effects of pollution, while a high frequency of passive, screen-based activities with the child does not moderate pollution effects.

title: On the Nature of the Firm: A Discussion on the Differences Between Chinese and American Firm
affiliations: Cheung Kong Graduate School of Business

detail.title: On the Nature of the Firm: A Discussion on the Differences Between Chinese and American Firm
detail.abstract: We first review the research topic of the 'nature of the firm' from an interdisciplinary perspective. Subsequently, we examine how the legal, business, organizational, and financial dimensions collectively shape the boundaries and practices of a firm from the perspectives of various stakeholders, including entrepreneurs, managers, and investors, and compare the differences between China and the United States in these aspects. The study demonstrates that cultural differences have a profound influence on corporate behavior, emphasizing the importance of cross-dimensional analysis in understanding corporate behavior and enhancing firm competitiveness.

detail.title: Human Rights, the Climate Emergency, and the Financial System

publicationDetails.detailsText: European Central Bank Legal Working Paper Series 2025/23
publicationDetails.journalName: European Central Bank Legal Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: On 9 April 2024, the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR) delivered a landmark ruling in Verein KlimaSeniorinnen Schweiz and Others v. Switzerland. The ruling was handed down together with two further rulings in Duarte Agostinho and others v. Portugal and others, and in Carême v. France. The ruling marked the first time the ECtHR held that insufficient climate action by a state constitutes a violation of human rights under the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR). While primarily having an impact on Switzerland as a defending State, the ruling is expected to indirectly affect the legal order of the European Union and its institutions. Moreover, the findings of the ECtHR have been reinforced by recent advisory opinions of other international courts and tribunals, in particular the opinion of the International Court of Justice, handed down on 23 July 2025. This paper first recalls the key facts and outcomes from each of the three ECtHR climate rulings and explores the key findings in greater detail. Second, the paper outlines the climate rulings of other international courts and tribunals. Thereafter, the paper explains the relevance of the KlimaSeniorinnen ruling for the Union and its institutions. First, as a matter of substance, the paper explains how the ruling carries lessons for the ambition and implementation of the climate policies of the Union and its Member States. Second, the paper goes on to explore the procedural avenues for litigants to bring an action before the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU), to challenge Union policies on the basis of the ECtHR’s ruling. The paper then outlines how the ruling may be relevant to the ECB, and for the national central banks (NCBs) and national competent authorities (NCAs) within the Eurosystem and Single Supervisory Mechanism. Finally, the paper explores how the ruling may be relevant to the financial sector, insofar as it increases the risk of litigation, and risks related to the process of adjustment towards a low-carbon economy (transition risk).

title: Assessing the impact of natural land on farmland value in Mediterranean EU countries
affiliations: Università degli Studi di Catania and Yale University - School of Forestry & Environmental Studies

detail.title: Assessing the impact of natural land on farmland value in Mediterranean EU countries
detail.abstract: There is limited empirical research on how natural land in the surrounding landscape affects farmland value. Drawing on a unique data set that combines farm-level information with land cover data within a 5 km radius of each farm, this study applies a hedonic approach to evaluate how natural land influences farmland values across five Euro-Mediterranean countries. We assess the effects of reallocating land between natural land types and between natural land and agriculture across all farms, as well as separately for crop farms and livestock farms. The results show that mixed forests, shrubland, and inland wetlands all provide positive externalities, whereas most other natural land types tend to reduce farmland value. These beneficial effects apply to crop farms, while the effect of natural land on livestock farms is generally negative. Overall, these results underscore the need for more targeted natural land management strategies that account for both land type and farming system.

title: The Value of Water Access Security in Agriculture
affiliations: Texas A&M University - College of Agriculture and Life Sciences, Texas A&M University, University of Georgia, affiliation not provided to SSRN and Texas A&M University

detail.title: The Value of Water Access Security in Agriculture
detail.abstract: Institutions are crucial for allocating natural resources. Surface water allocation in the western U.S. follows the prior appropriation doctrine, which distributes water based on the date when water was first appropriated for beneficial use. During scarcity, water is allocated by seniority, with holders of more junior rights losing access first. Curtailments of water access influence the profitability of irrigated production, especially in the arid West where most croplands depend on irrigation. The Ricardian theory of rent suggests a premium for senior water rights, as the net present value of long-term returns is higher due to more secure access. We estimate this premium using a hedonic pricing model and agricultural land transactions as proxies for water-rights values. Our dataset links roughly 25,000 sales across 37 Colorado counties with geocoded information on associated water rights. Results show that surface-water access increases land values by about $6,300 per acre, or 64 % relative to similar non-irrigated parcels. Furthermore, we estimate the premium for properties that are one year more senior in water rights to be about $49 per acre. Our results also indicate that properties with access to storage and supplementary groundwater rights sell, on average, for 16% and 14% more, respectively, compared to irrigated properties with only surface water access. These findings highlight the importance of water security in shaping agricultural land markets and offer insights into how policy measures, such as expanding water markets or investing in storage reservoirs, can potentially improve allocation and reduce vulnerability of irrigated agriculture.

title: The Impact of Artificial Intelligence on Human Rights in Nigeria: Conflict or Consonance
affiliations: Lead City University

detail.title: The Impact of Artificial Intelligence on Human Rights in Nigeria: Conflict or Consonance
detail.abstract:
This work examines human rights in Nigeria, the meaning of Artificial Intelligence and its existence in Nigeria, whilst also examining its positive and negative influence on specifically highlighted fundamental rights recognized internationally and in the Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria. 

This work concludes by drawing a resolution on how the concept of artificial intelligence conflicts with some constitutionally-protected human rights in Nigeria but also how there is a future capable of accommodating a consonance between both, and this work dishes two fundamental recommendations to arrive at this desired consonance.

affiliations: , University of Chitral and Shaheed Benazir Bhutto Women University

detail.title: Energy Productivity and Economic Growth Nexus: A Case Study of Pakistan from 1990-2018
detail.abstract: This study investigates the relationship between energy and economic growth in Pakistan from 1990 to 2018. Using Gross Domestic Product (GDP) as the dependent variable, the study examines the effects of gross fixed capital formation, labor productivity, energy balance, oil prices, and Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) in the energy sector as independent variables. The analytical framework employs the Auto Regressive Distributed Lag (ARDL) Model, while the stability of variables is assessed through CUSUM and CUSUM Square tests. Key findings reveal that labor force participation in the energy sector and rising oil prices have a sustained negative impact on economic growth. Conversely, gross fixed capital formation positively influences GDP both in the short and long term. Interestingly, FDI in the energy sector shows a negative effect on GDP in the short term but a positive effect in the long term. The study emphasizes the need for a comprehensive transformation of Pakistan's energy sector. It recommends a strategic shift from hydrocarbon-based energy to hydropower to stabilize oil prices and achieve significant, sustainable production increases in the long term. These findings provide critical insights into Pakistan's energy economic relationship, offering valuable guidance for policymakers, scholars, and industry stakeholders.

reference: Taxation of Trusts, Foundations and Similar Arrangements in a Global Setting
title: Trusts and Taxes on Wealth
affiliations: Universidad Carlos III de Madrid

detail.title: Trusts and Taxes on Wealth

declarations.funderStatement: I acknowledge the support provided by the research project titled “La necesaria actualización de los sistemas tributarios ante los retos del S. XXI (XXITAX)”. Prometeo 2021-041, Generalitat Valenciana, directed by Alfredo García Prats. This work is also aligned with the Acción estratégica, directed by the author, titled “Los sistemas financiero y tributario en un entorno multinivel: diseño constitucional, aplicación práctica, distribución de competencias”. Ref: 2022/00517/001

publicationDetails.detailsText: Taxation of Trusts, Foundations and Similar Arrangements in a Global Setting

detail.abstract:
Recent proposals for a global wealth tax have revitalized long-standing debates about how to design such taxes. The discussion is particularly difficult because these are taxes that have been abandoned by most of our neighboring countries with high taxation systems (OECD members, EU countries). This means that there are not many useful examples today. In addition, a striking aspect of the proposals is that the element of legal design is often absent. Consequently, the central aspect of any wealth tax, which is defining wealth for legal purposes and measuring its amount, does not appear among the core elements of the proposals.

This chapter examines some of the issues that arise when trying to design a comprehensive wealth tax which may be applied to different legal structures. A key element lies in the different conceptions of property that are evident in specific legal structures, such as trusts and similar arrangements, and the challenge that this poses for this type of taxes. In particular, the focus will be on Trust structures, which are notably difficult to compare across countries, or even within one jurisdiction, as they often respond to very different logics and interests.

The chapter will first (II) tackle the current debate on wealth taxation and assess some of the main proposals. The proposals are very different, and it does not help that wealth taxes have become a rare breed, which in turn encourages creativity, not always helpful for the sake of comparisons, in the different proposed taxes. It will then (III) examine the challenges of subjecting trust structures to a net wealth tax. Trusts, often used as vehicles for managing and “protecting” family wealth, present unique difficulties in determining ownership and tax liability, as well as international recognition issues. In practice, the various and varying purposes of trusts, from charitable to discretionary inter alia, will often complicate their treatment under a wealth tax regime. Finally, (IV) the chapter explores examples of existing wealth taxes in different jurisdictions and discuss the constitutional and practical challenges that have arisen.

Although this chapter does not focus on any specific country, particular attention will be paid to the Spanish case, as it does remain one of the few jurisdictions that has managed to not fully eliminate a net wealth tax, which has undergone a particular reform in recent times. This makes it a test bed, not necessarily a positive one, for the kind of problems posed by these taxes and by ownership unbundling structures such as trusts.

title: Beliefs, Information Trust, and Air Pollution

detail.title: Beliefs, Information Trust, and Air Pollution
detail.abstract: This paper examines how the quality of disclosures shapes public trust in official data. Using daily emission records from waste-to-energy plants in China (2020-2022) and housing data from 92 cities, I estimate pollution beliefs through a residential sorting model. Households perceive higher and more uncertain emissions when records are flawed, despite technical explanations of the flaws. There is limited evidence of manipulation by plants, suggesting fundamental distrust. The estimated household's annual willingness to pay for a 1% improvement in information quality is $1.23. The results show that low-quality disclosure discounts the value of information and erodes information trust.

title: Measuring Acquisition-led Growth as a Rising Corporate Strategy
affiliations: University of Geneva

detail.title: Measuring Acquisition-led Growth as a Rising Corporate Strategy
detail.abstract: This paper argues that mergers and acquisitions (M&A) have become a primary corporate growth strategy for U.S. non-financial corporations and should be treated as investment from the firm's perspective. Using Compustat firm-level data (1980-2019), I document a compositional shift from productive assets toward goodwill and other intangibles, with goodwill surpassing 15% of total assets among large acquirers. When total investment is measured as capital expenditures plus acquisition outlays in real terms, the common time-series component shows no secular decline. Acquisition activity is highly concentrated: the top decile accounts for over 90% of spending. These "high acquirers" grow assets 14-16 percentage points faster and sales 5-9 points faster than other firms; the growth premium vanishes when firms are grouped by accumulated intangibles (excluding goodwill), indicating that the advantage reflects acquisition intensity rather than intangible stocks. Post-2000, acquisition intensity becomes a stronger predictor than capital expenditures of entering the top decile by assets, sales, and sales-weighted markups. Markups and profit shares concentrate at the top: the profit share of the top decile of acquirers rises from 24% in the 1980s to 51% by 2008-2020. I propose a framework that links acquisition-led growth to four stylized facts-measured investment stagnation, rising concentration, higher markups, and profit concentration-and discuss implications for measurement and merger policy.

title: Economic Policy Uncertainty and Accounting Reporting Complexity
affiliations: Liverpool John Moores University, Colorado State University, Fort Collins - Department of Accounting, University of Roehampton and Loughborough University

detail.title: Economic Policy Uncertainty and Accounting Reporting Complexity

publicationDetails.detailsText: Forthcoming, Journal of Accounting, Auditing and Finance

detail.abstract: We posit that accounting reporting complexity includes two components-monetary reporting complexity (MRC) and textual reporting complexity (TRC). It is generally challenging to disentangle these components because they tend to increase with real business activities. Economic policy uncertainty (EPU) provides an ideal setting to overcome this challenge. Greater EPU reduces real business activities, suggesting a reduction in MRC. However, TRC can increase or decrease depending on disclosure incentives. Using monetary and textual eXtensible Business Reporting Language (XBRL) tags to measure MRC and TRC, respectively, we find that high EPU reduces MRC but increases TRC. These findings survive a series of robustness checks. Additional analyses show that [1] these relationships hold for all ten policy categories; [2] the reduction in five hard-to-reverse business activities drives the reduction in MRC; [3] the decrease in MRC drives the increase in TRC; [4] the simultaneous changes in MRC and TRC help reduce the increase in information asymmetry due to high EPU; and [5] these relationships are stronger for firms relying more on the government for their operations and weaker for firms with high political risk or proprietary risk. Collectively, these results suggest that, when facing greater uncertainty about future economic policies, firms tend to delay real economic activities and justify this reduction using textual disclosure. Our study makes several contributions to research on economic policy uncertainty and accounting reporting complexity.

title: Race, Violence, and the Effectiveness of Protest
affiliations: University of Rochester - Department of Political Science, Hebrew University of Jerusalem - Hebrew University, Tel Aviv University, Ben Gurion University of the Negev,  Columbia University, Department of Political Science, Students , Harvard University - Havard Keneddy School and Harvard University - Havard Keneddy School

detail.title: Race, Violence, and the Effectiveness of Protest
detail.abstract: Protests constitute a primary way that members of the public express their preferences and seek to change public policy. Focusing on policy protests in the United States, we develop hypotheses about the impact of protesters’ race (Black or white) and violent disruptive tactics on the effectiveness of protests. We test our predictions with parallel experiments that expose citizens, individuals affiliated with civic organizations, and public officials to protest scenarios. We find that violent protests generate disapproval but also, perhaps surprisingly, policy responsiveness.  These relationships hold regardless of the race of the protesters. When it comes to nonviolent protests, however, race fundamentally matters and in countervailing ways. Black nonviolent protesters receive less approval than white nonviolent protesters, but they also are the only ones to generate policy responsiveness. These findings suggest that assertions about the relative impact of violent or nonviolent protests need to consider the identity of the protesters given that not all nonviolent protests are treated equally.

title: Guidance on the Environmental Conditions of Detention
affiliations: University of Edinburgh School of Law and University of Edinburgh

detail.title: Guidance on the Environmental Conditions of Detention

publicationDetails.detailsText: Edinburgh School of Law Research Paper No. 2025.27
publicationDetails.journalName: University of Edinburgh School of Law Legal Studies Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
‘Environmental conditions’ refer in particular to the sensory environment in places of detention. Four aspects are discussed here: sound, light, temperature and air. ‘Detention’ means any situation in which people are deprived of their liberty. These environmental conditions of detention cover prisons, remand centres, and secure accommodation for children. They are also relevant for other sites of detention, such as asylum reception centres, hospitals and care homes when detention is mandated. This brief offers clarity on how existing rules of detention apply and explains why the environmental conditions of detention warrant further consideration.

Often, places of detention have been constructed without due consideration of the importance of our immediate environment, and this potential for harm. The combined impact of poor environmental conditions may in fact constitute cruel, inhuman and degrading treatment as defined in international law. In addition, manipulation of environmental and sensory conditions has often been used intentionally as a method of torture. Poor environmental conditions can also exacerbate the impact of other methods of torture and ill-treatment.
